newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-EMU delay preferable to weak Euro - Jochimsen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMU delay preferable to weak Euro - Jochimsen.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said on Monday the prospect of a weak single European currency was worse than delaying its launch.
Addressing a news conference, Jochimsen rejected a recent statement by Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel who said the point of no return for starting monetary union had already been reached.
"I believe the point of no return will not be reached until 1998," said Jochimsen, who is also president of the state central bank of North Rhine-Westphalia.
The European Union decides in the spring of 1998 on the basis of 1997 statistics which countries qualify for monetary union, scheduled to be launched in 1999.
Jochimsen warned against watering down the criteria to allow a large group of countries to take part and said awareness was waning of the need for a strict application of the convergence criteria.
He also attacked the EU Commission for reportedly paying experts to play down the risks involved in adopting the euro.
Recent volatility in financial markets stemmed in part from uncertainty over whether the choice of members will be a political decision or based on economic fundamentals, he said.

While the Maastricht Treaty did not demand that countries achieve an exact "point landing" on the criteria, any leeway for allowing an overshoot of the reference levels must focus on assessing if the convergence achieved was solid and lasting.

Jochimsen noted that Germany met neither the debt nor the deficit criteria for monetary union in 1996. Its public debt had last year even moved further above the Maastricht ceiling of 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), he said.
"Solid material foundations for monetary union are indispensable," Jochimsen said.

"If after the start of monetary union it turns out that the foundations do not yet support -- if the euro either fails, drifts apart, or becomes a weak currency -- the damage to European integration would be far worse than for example a limited and conditional postponement."
Any interpretation of the criteria must not be generous and countries must not be allowed to resort to creative accounting to qualify for the euro, Jochimsen said.
"The fact that this awareness is less and less prevalent is definitely not helping monetary union gain the necessary credibility among citizens," Jochimsen said.

"And if the EU Commission, as recently reported in the press, makes a whole series of secret arrangements with 170 scientists and high-ranking experts to talk down the risks under the pretext of giving objective information and in return for payment from EU funds, then - I want to put it very mildly - that is most definitely not the right way to solve the problem..."
Such a move was not suited to winning the confidence of citizens or of markets for the euro, he said.
Jochimsen also said Britain's move last week to increase the independence of the Bank of England did not on its own mean the country had made a fundamental step towards joining EMU.
"It was a brave and quick decision but it doesn't give the Bank of England the level of independence required by the Maastricht treaty.
"Basic interests have not been changed. It is much too early to draw conclusions from this."
Britain's new Labour government last week gave the central bank independence to set interest rates but kept responsibility for setting the inflation target.
Jochimsen also said a rise in German interest rates was not needed at present although a further strengthening of the dollar against the mark in the long term would cause price pressures.
